notes.meaning: Solomon began building the temple in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah. This was the hill where God had appeared to David to stop a deadly plague, and ancient Jewish tradition held it was the same spot where Abraham prepared to offer Isaac. By building here, Solomon showed that worship is founded on God's chosen place of mercy and sacrifice rather than human convenience.

Work officially began on the second day of the second month during Solomon's fourth year as king. The first three years were not wasted, but were spent gathering materials and organizing large teams of workers. Careful planning and patient preparation are often necessary before doing a great work for God.

Solomon laid the foundation using the older standard of measurement from the time of Moses. The main building was sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, which was twice the size of the earlier tabernacle tent. Following God's established plans showed respect for divine order in worship.

The front porch stretched across the entire width of the temple, measuring twenty cubits long. Solomon covered the inside of this entryway with pure gold. This bright, gleaming entrance prepared worshipers to step into a place dedicated entirely to God's glory.

Solomon paneled the walls of the main room, called the Holy Place, with cypress wood and covered them with fine gold. Artists carved figures of palm trees and chains into the paneling. These carvings brought reminders of life, fruitfulness, and beauty into God's dwelling place.

The Chronicler notes that the temple was decorated with precious stones for beauty and with high-grade gold brought from Parvaim. The stones added color and sparkle against the golden walls. Offering such costly materials reflected the high honor due to God.

Every part of the room was overlaid with gold, including the ceiling beams, doorposts, walls, and doors. Carvings of cherubim, powerful winged angels who serve God, covered the walls. Walking into the room gave priests a sense of entering the heavenly courts where angels constantly worship the Lord.

Solomon built the Most Holy Place, the inner room where God's special presence rested, as a perfect square twenty cubits wide and twenty cubits long. He lined the walls with six hundred talents of fine gold, which was an enormous amount of wealth. The hidden perfection and splendor of this room showed that God's greatest glory is holy and pure.

Even the nails used to secure the gold sheets were made of solid gold, each weighing fifty shekels. Solomon also overlaid the upper chambers and ceiling area with gold. Every detail, even small fasteners and high ceilings rarely seen by human eyes, was completed with excellence for God.

Inside the Most Holy Place, Solomon placed two large statues of cherubim covered in gold. These were not the small figures mounted directly on the ark of the covenant, but massive new statues built to stand inside the larger room. They represented the heavenly hosts who attend the presence of God.

Each cherub had two wings measuring five cubits each, creating a total wingspan of twenty cubits across the room. Their outer wings touched the side walls, and their inner wings met in the center above the ark. They stood upright on their feet facing outward toward the main room, appearing like ready servants waiting on God rather than idols to be worshiped.

Solomon made a thick curtain, or veil, woven from fine linen in royal blue, purple, and crimson, decorated with cherubim patterns. This veil hung between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place to mark the boundary around God's holy presence. Christians remember that this temple curtain was torn apart at the death of Jesus, opening the way for everyone to draw near to God.

Two tall bronze pillars were placed in front of the temple porch, measuring thirty-five cubits in combined height, each topped with a carved crown called a capital. These towering columns stood out boldly before the building. Their impressive size announced the strength and dignity of the sanctuary behind them.

Artisans created woven metal chains to wrap around the pillar tops like decorative wreaths, hanging one hundred bronze pomegranates from the chains. The pomegranates and chainwork gave the capitals a rich, ornate finish. In Scripture, fruit designs often pointed to God's blessing, life, and abundance.

Solomon set up the two pillars at the temple entrance, naming the southern one Jachin, meaning 'He shall establish,' and the northern one Boaz, meaning 'In Him is strength.' Worshipers saw these meaningful names every time they arrived to pray and bring sacrifices. The pillars stood as constant reminders that God establishes His people and gives them the strength to stand.
